title: Selection makes organisms only as perfect as their local competitors

fields.label: Label
fields.value: Selection makes organisms only as perfect as their local competitors

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: Natural selection only makes each organism as perfect as, or slightly more perfect than, the other inhabitants of its own country, so endemic species of a region such as New Zealand may yield to species introduced from a larger region.

fields.label: Work
fields.value: On the Origin of Species by Means of Natural Selection, or the Preservation of Favoured Races in the Struggle for Life

fields.label: Quotation
fields.value: Natural selection tends only to make each organic being as perfect as, or slightly more perfect than, the other inhabitants of the same country with which it has to struggle for existence.

fields.label: Agent
fields.value: delphisci Origin of Species claim extractor

fields.label: Assumptions
fields.value: Charles Darwin, On the Origin of Species (1st ed., London: John Murray, 1859), Chapter VI, “Difficulties on Theory”; section “Organs not in all cases absolutely perfect.”. Scope: inhabitants of regions, especially islands vs continents

fields.label: Assessment
fields.value: GPT-5.6 Sol on darwin1859-ch06-14: partially-resolvable, resolvability 0.69

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Large invasion datasets support broad tests of the island-versus-mainland implication. They test a proxy for local competitive adaptation, not perfection itself or its exclusive production by selection.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Compare establishment, displacement, abundance, and performance of introduced versus endemic species across islands and continents while controlling for propagule pressure and environment. Systematic competitive replacement supports the prediction; endemic superiority under matched conditions opposes it.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Propagule pressure and human disturbance confound competitive superiority.

'Perfect' has no single measurable scale.

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Open invasion and threat data can test the prediction that endemics of smaller regions yield to species from larger ones, and that analysis is standard. They do not measure degree of perfection or show that selection stopped at the local competitor. Discriminating power is limited by human-mediated confounds, so the result speaks to a restricted biogeographic proxy.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Compare establishment and impact of species moved from larger biotas into smaller ones, including islands such as New Zealand, with the reverse direction. Systematic yielding of local endemics to invaders from richer biotas supports the biogeographic prediction; equal or reversed success would count against it.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
'As perfect as local competitors' is not itself a measured variable; establishment is a proxy.

Invasion success is confounded by propagule pressure, disturbance, and enemy release, not only relative perfection.

GloNAF covers plants, while the claim is about inhabitants in general.
